Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
try hard not think about the trauma

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, sexual situations and being around children are hard-to-explain triggers in the absence of any related trauma content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on generic hyperarousal/dissociation and transportation-related cues, so these two triggers do not fit the trauma-specific pattern and weaken Triggers → Threat / Triggers → Memory coherence.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: Humiliation can occur after an MVC, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals otherwise suggest self-blame and social disconnection, yet no memory, threat, or trigger content reflects embarrassment, public exposure, disability, or shame-linked reminders. For this trauma type, permanent humiliation is insufficiently supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is poorly linked to the rest of the formulation. The profile’s active threat content is hyperarousal/startle and dissociative memory disturbance, and the selected strategies otherwise involve vigilance and situational avoidance. Undereating does not plausibly address any represented symptom cluster and feels disconnected from the threat/memory/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: 'Being around children' is a weak fit as a trauma trigger for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless the crash specifically involved children; nothing else in the profile supports children as a salient cue, so this trigger appears disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is possible but is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a motor vehicle collision. The accompanying appraisals are self-blame and alienation, but there are no other items suggesting shame/humiliation themes (e.g., social exposure, moral failure, visible disgrace), making this appraisal stand out as poorly integrated.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: 'Avoid open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on transportation cues, startle/physical threat reactions, and trauma memory phenomena from an MVC. Open-space avoidance suggests a different threat pattern (e.g., assault/agoraphobic vulnerability) that is not represented elsewhere.

A bicycle-specific trigger is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless the collision specifically involved a bicycle; the rest of the profile is vehicle/crash focused rather than bicycle focused, so this item stands out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: Alarm to unexpected touch suggests an interpersonal/assault-related threat cue more than a motor vehicle collision. In the context of the other threat items, generic startle and physical reactivity fit, but touch-specific alarm is not well linked to the reported trauma or the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is a broad social-identity appraisal that is not impossible, but it sits awkwardly with the otherwise self-blame/competence-focused appraisal pattern tied to an MVC. It is less clearly connected to the memory and trigger content than more trauma-specific appraisals would be.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not impossible, but here it is poorly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links threat and appraisals to maladaptive strategies, and the other strategies are vehicle avoidance and thought monitoring, whereas undereating addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

vignette:
Raymond is a 67-year-old widowed military medic who presented for his initial evaluation carrying the particular composure of a man long accustomed to holding himself together under pressure. He had spent decades in uniform, trained to stay functional when others could not, and that identity had shaped not only his career but his understanding of himself. What brought him to the clinic was a motor vehicle collision that occurred fourteen months ago, on a rain-slicked highway outside the city where he now lives alone, and which had undone something in him that he had not yet been able to name.

The accident happened on a Friday evening. Raymond had been driving home from a veterans' social function and a car traveling at speed ran a red light and struck his vehicle broadside with enough force to spin it across two lanes. In the immediate aftermath, before he lost consciousness briefly, he registered the smell - alcohol on the breath of the other driver, who had stumbled toward him through broken glass, and beneath that the acrid, unmistakable odor of something burning near the engine. Raymond had triaged casualties in combat. He had worked on bodies in conditions most people cannot imagine. But lying there in his own damaged vehicle, the smells reaching him before his vision fully cleared, something in his professional composure simply failed to hold.

In the weeks that followed, Raymond noticed that the experience would not settle into the past the way he expected it to. When he tried to describe what had happened - to his physician, to his adult daughter on the phone - he would begin coherently and then lose the thread entirely, the account fragmenting mid-sentence until he fell silent. The memory itself felt strange to him, dissociated in a way he found deeply unsettling: as though the event had happened to someone he had watched rather than to himself. Yet when the memory arrived uninvited, it brought sound with it - the impact, the grinding of metal, the voice of the other driver - playing back with a vividness that the rest of the memory seemed to lack.

Raymond had come to believe, with a quiet certainty that he rarely spoke aloud, that the accident had happened because of something he had done - a choice, a moment of inattention, a failure of the vigilance he had always prided himself on. Alongside this sat a deeper and more corrosive conviction: that he could no longer trust himself to respond correctly when it mattered. For a man whose professional identity rested entirely on competence under pressure, he had come to regard himself as weak in a way that felt both shameful and irrefutable.

His work as a medic had not stopped after the collision, but it had changed in ways that were becoming difficult to conceal. He no longer drove himself to assignments and had arranged increasingly elaborate workarounds to avoid being a passenger in vehicles as well, limiting his radius of movement and declining callouts that required transport. When a colleague's jacket carried the faint smell of alcohol at a training day, Raymond felt his body respond before his mind had processed the stimulus - his chest tightening, his hands unsteady, a physical alarm that seemed entirely disproportionate and that he found mortifying. Ordinary sounds - a door slamming in an adjacent room, a vehicle backfiring in the parking lot - would cause him to startle visibly, and he had begun timing his arrivals and departures to minimize encounters with colleagues who might notice.

At home, he worked constantly to keep his thoughts away from the accident, monitoring them with an exhausting vigilance and redirecting them the moment the collision began to surface. He had begun to worry that this monitoring itself was a sign of something worse - that the effort required to stay on the right side of his own mind meant he was closer to losing it than anyone around him knew.

What finally brought Raymond in was a conversation with his daughter, who told him plainly that she was frightened for him. He had not driven to see her in nearly a year. He arrived at the clinic hoping, above all, to understand whether what was happening to him was something a man in his position could recover from - and afraid, in equal measure, that the answer would confirm what he had already begun to suspect about himself.
